world.title: The pipeline built in the 1980s to survive a closed Hormuz was shut by drones from Iraq.

items.html: Saudi Arabia suspended the East-West pipeline on 13 September after a drone strike Saudi authorities traced to Maysan province in south-eastern Iraq, near the Iranian border. The 1,200km line normally carries 4–5m barrels a day against a 7m maximum, running crude to Yanbu on the Red Sea. It exists precisely to bypass the Strait of Hormuz — and Hormuz flows are already down to roughly 6–9m bpd from over a fifth of global supply. Repairs are estimated at five to six weeks. Brent went above $105 and was quoted near $108. Both the chokepoint and its designed alternative are impaired at once.

Anthropic's Dario Amodei published an essay urging AI companies to deliberately slow the development of more capable models, and Sam Altman agreed. Semiconductors sold off — Nvidia, SK Hynix and Samsung futures all lower — and technology closed the worst sector at −1.49%. President Trump responded on Truth Social that the only guardrails needed are a 'STRONG AND SMART' president. The market's read was not that AI is over but that the capex cycle might slow, which is why Alphabet and Meta rose while the chipmakers fell — and why Palantir, which sells governance rather than compute, rose 3.64%.

The FOMC decides Wednesday 16 September with a hike above 90% priced. The Bank of Japan decides Friday 18 September with a hike from 1.00% to 1.25% 97% priced. Triple witching is the same Friday. Two central banks tightening inside three days, the second landing on the largest options expiry of the quarter, into a dealer book that is short gamma. A decision priced above 90% has an asymmetric surprise: the damage is in a hold, not a hike.

world.note: The through-line: the oil shock is feeding the inflation print that is feeding the rate decision. Petrol added 3.9% in August and took the headline with it. Wednesday is the Fed responding to a supply shock it cannot reach with a policy rate.

stance.title: The regime was right all week and it did not save a single position.

items.html: Policy Tightening, week 2. Friday's 3.4% CPI widened the binding gate's cushion rather than narrowing it, and Monday agreed: a 5% ten-year, a 52-week high in the two-year, a hike above 90% priced. Nothing argues against the regime. The regime simply had nothing to say about a fee-guidance cut or a seven-cent stop miss.

Net gamma −$37.62B — a 10 September figure, four sessions old, because the clone cannot be refreshed. Treat the level as indicative and the sign as the only tradeable part. Negative gamma into an FOMC decision tomorrow and a triple witching on Friday is the structural fact of this week.

Heat went 3.15R on Friday, 2.00R after the stops, and 3.00R once OKTA was on — back to a 3.0R cap. The round trip took one session. Nothing here is over the line, but the book is carrying full risk into a Fed decision tomorrow and a triple witching on Friday, with the newest position three days old. No room for another.

Two of the three positions in this book moved on Monday for the same reason. PLTR rose 3.64% on AI governance and OKTA 11.98% on the security bid — both are the Amodei essay, priced two different ways. AAPL, up 0.24%, is the only position not attached to it. That is not sector concentration, which a screener would catch; it is narrative concentration, which nothing in Phoenix measures. If Wednesday's Fed takes the tape back, or the safety story fades as quickly as it arrived, two thirds of the book moves down together.

Every one of these exits happened at the original stop. Nothing was widened, nothing was talked out of, nothing was averaged down. Two of them were losses and all three were correct executions — that distinction is the only part of this week that was under your control, and it went the right way.

stance.note: The honest read on the stance: it was right about rates and right about the direction of policy, and positions sized against that thesis still lost. Regime calls set the odds over a season. They do not immunise single names over three sessions.

macro.title: Five percent printed on the ten-year, and the pipeline built to avoid Hormuz is shut.

items.html: Phoenix has the ten-year at 4.94%, +11bp on the day, +15bp on the week and +26bp on the month; the two-year at 4.43%; the 2s10s curve at 51bp; the real ten-year at 2.46%. Monday's tape went well past all of it: the ten-year touched 5.00% intraday, the first time since October 2023, and closed 4.999%; the two-year set a 52-week high at 4.658%; the thirty-year held 5.354%. The front end moving with the long end is the market repricing the policy path, not term premium.

A hike on Wednesday is now priced above 90%, from 85-86% after Friday's CPI and roughly 70% before it. August CPI was +0.4% on the month and +3.4% on the year, both in line; core was +0.3%, a tenth above forecast, and +2.4% annually. Petrol did much of the headline work — up 3.9% to $4.28 a gallon on the Middle East — while shelter reaccelerated to +0.3% from +0.1%. The core detail is what moved the odds.

The pack's ten-year tracks daily. us02, real10 and hy still do not — all three read 0bp on the day for a sixth session — and hy is still quoted in percent rather than basis points. With the clone frozen, every one of these is Thursday's. Read the front end and credit at weekly resolution at best.

The dollar index closed near 99.5, up about 0.4%, on the yield move. USDJPY was ~154.3, off session highs near 154.9 — the yen gave back ground on Monday after four weeks of strength, which matters because the Bank of Japan decides Friday 18 September with a move from 1.00% to 1.25% 97% priced. Estimates put the yen carry trade at $764bn to $1.1tn. A BoJ hike landing on triple-witching Friday is the single most avoidable risk on this week's calendar.

High yield at 271bp once the unit switch is undone — inside the 300bp line that separates calm from watchful, and it has not moved through a week that produced a 5% ten-year. Credit is not pricing distress, which is worth holding onto: nothing that happened to this book was systemic. It is also Thursday's figure.

Phoenix has WTI at 102.48, +23.17% on the month. Monday's tape: WTI +2.25% to $102.30, Brent above $105 and quoted as high as $108, after Friday's brief dip under $100. Gold fell 1.76% to $4,331.40 — a geopolitical shock that pushed gold down, because real yields did the deciding. Bitcoin rose about 2.2% to ~$79,000.

macro.note: The gates. Three of four hold. CPI y/y at 3.3 clears its 2.5 threshold by 0.8 on Phoenix's stale figure and by more on Friday's 3.4 print; the real ten-year's three-month change at 33bp clears by 8bp; drawdown clears by 9.51. items.html: This brief reported Gabriel's PLTR position as live on 11 September and again earlier this morning. It was not — it stopped out on Thursday 10 September. The reason is a method error, not a data gap: I was checking the closing price against the stop. PLTR closed Thursday at 165.86, comfortably above 164.62, and I wrote that the stop could not be confirmed. Its low that day was 164.55. A stop is an order that fills on the low, not a level tested at 4pm, and every position line in every brief before this one was checked the wrong way. From here the book is reconciled against intraday lows since entry, and the two remaining positions have been re-checked on that basis: GOOG's lowest bar since entry is 324.41 against a 305.67 stop, AAPL's is 309.90 against 301.99.

PLTR closes below its stop — the condition was written wrong. It never closed below its stop and it stopped out anyway. Written against a close, it was never capable of firing on the event it existed to catch. Replacing it: conditions on positions are now written against the low, and the diff should be too.

August CPI at or below 3.0% — FAILED, closed Friday. It printed 3.4% and the binding gate's cushion widened rather than narrowed. No dovish argument is left and Wednesday is above 90% priced. Retired.

BoJ hikes and USDJPY below 150 — still not met, and the yen went the wrong way. USDJPY was ~154.3 on Monday, off session highs near 154.9, after four weeks of yen strength. The decision is Friday 18 September, 97% priced. Carried forward.

The BAC exit was not on any condition list either. No invalidation condition here has ever pointed at a bank's fee guidance, because the thesis was macro — higher rates, wider margins — and the macro was right on the day the position died. A CEO speaking at a conference in the week before a quarter closes is a scheduled, knowable event. It belongs on the calendar.

invalidation.title: The Fed decides tomorrow and there is nothing to do before it.

items.html: The AI-safety bid unwinds and takes two positions with it. PLTR and OKTA both rose on Monday on the same essay, and OKTA rose 11.98% on it in a single session. The arithmetic to hold onto: the entry at 182.73 is 9.75% above Friday's close and the stop at 162.61 is 2.34% below it, so the whole risk unit is Monday's move plus a sliver. If OKTA simply round-trips to where it traded on Friday, the position is −0.81R and the stop has not been touched. A 12% one-day move that is three days old can give all of that back in one session, and this one is not on the calendar — which is exactly what made BAC expensive.

The FOMC holds on Wednesday instead of hiking. Above 90% priced, so the surprise is one-sided. In a market short gamma by $37.6B — a stale figure, but the sign is not in doubt — a hold produces a rally larger than the news deserves and would be the first real challenge to POLICY_TIGHTENING since the regime was set on 31 August.

The Bank of Japan hikes on Friday into triple witching. 97% priced, 1.00% to 1.25%, on a carry position estimated at $764bn to $1.1tn, with USDJPY back at ~154.3 rather than the sub-150 this brief has been watching for. The risk is not the hike — it is the hike landing on the quarter's largest expiry while dealers are short gamma.

weekly.headline: The week the Fed stopped arguing with itself — and Palantir walked to its stop
weekly.standfirst: Four sessions, because Monday was Labor Day, and the index gave up about 0.6% across them — the third week running in which a great deal happened and the S&P barely moved. Underneath: crude through $100 on Saudi production at its lowest since 1990, the ten-year up 15bp to 4.94% with the thirty-year at levels last seen in June 2007, the VIX out of a 28-session range, and dealer gamma collapsing to −$44B before recovering. CPI then printed 3.4% in line on Friday and put a September hike at 85.6%, killing the dovish case this brief had been testing since 4 September. In the book AAPL turned green on a doubled revenue estimate and PLTR ended the week 0.75% above its stop after a Citigroup downgrade — whether it held is the open question of the weekend. Heat 3.15R against 3.0R.

The figure is recomputed per account: the pack reports 7.19R because _pk_portfolio sums both books and divides by one account's capital, which is the bug Gabriel caught on 9 September. Columns are the week to 2026-09-10 and entry-to-date; marks are Thursday's close because Friday is not yet in the engine.

The week's real event is a level, not a return. PLTR closed Thursday at 165.86, 0.85% above its stop, after Citigroup cut it to Market Perform on a P/E near 142 and BTIG went Neutral. Friday's close is not in Phoenix and I could not source one, so whether that stop held is the open question of the weekend. The Nasdaq rose 0.88% on the day, which makes a stop-out the less likely outcome — but 0.85% is inside this stock's ordinary intraday range, and if it has gone, heat falls to roughly 2.15R without a decision being made.

A Fed that stopped arguing with itself, and a stock that walked to its stop

1. The inflation question closed. CPI printed 3.4%% year over year against the 3.0%% test this brief had set as the first argument against POLICY_TIGHTENING — and it moved up from 3.3, not down. Odds of a hike at the 16 September meeting went from a coin flip a week earlier, to roughly 70%% on Thursday, to 85.6%% after the print. The regime's binding gate now clears its threshold by 0.9. There is no dovish case left to argue.

2. Dealer gamma collapsed and then partly recovered. Net gamma went −$3.98B on Tuesday, −$26.05B on Wednesday, −$44.19B on Thursday and −$37.62B in the latest pack. The index lost its 50-day on Thursday for the first time in this run. Friday's 1.06% rally on an in-line print is what that positioning does to ordinary news — and the same multiplier is pointed at Wednesday's decision. Phoenix's own diff never flagged any of it, because it tests for a sign flip and the sign was already negative.

3. Two positions resolved in opposite directions. AAPL launched the iPhone Duo at $1,999 — under the $2,000-plus that had been trailed — shipping 23 October, and the stock shrugged until Deepwater doubled its estimate of the Duo's share of fiscal 2027 iPhone revenue from 5%% to 10%%, sending it up 3.56%% and turning the position green. PLTR went the other way on a Citigroup downgrade, closing the week on its stop. Both were sell-side opinions rather than company news, which is worth noting: the book's two biggest moves this week came from analysts, not from the businesses.

4. Alphabet acquired a court. A US appeals court cleared 2,400–3,000-plus youth-addiction suits against Google, Meta, Snapchat and TikTok to proceed, and refused to delay the trial brought by 29 state attorneys general. That is materially larger than the FTC's YouTube probe this brief had been tracking, which remains unfiled after sixteen days. GOOG fell 2.09%% on the ruling and still finished the week as the book's steadiest name.

Oil stopped being a risk premium and became a supply number

WTI settled above $102 on Thursday and Brent reached $107.63, both through $100 for the first time since May, before Friday took WTI back to $99.05. The move was not a headline premium: Saudi Arabia reported production at its lowest level since 1990 after Houthi strikes on energy facilities including the 400,000 barrel-a-day Jazan refinery, and roughly ten commodity ships a day are crossing the Strait of Hormuz against a chokepoint that carries a fifth of world oil in peacetime. US petrol averaged $4.27 and diesel set a record.

The transmission into this book runs crude → CPI → the regime gate, and it worked all week. It also showed up somewhere more concrete: seven of the eight names in Phoenix's screener are now oil or marine shipping — DK, PBR, BP and PSX alongside BWLP, DAC and NMM. The war has stopped being a macro input and become what the screener returns. None of it is actionable while heat is over cap, and the screener has still reached nothing at its 20-bar horizon, so the verdict remains INSUFFICIENT.

Friday's 3.35%% fall in crude is the first thing to challenge that in two weeks. One down day from $102 is not a supply story ending.

Two central banks and an expiry, into a market that magnifies all three

FOMCFederal Reserve decision — a hike is 85.6% pricedWed2026-09-16
BOJBank of Japan decision — a hike is 97% pricedthis week2026-09-18
OPEXTriple witching — quarterly expiryFri2026-09-18

The Fed is the week. With a hike 85.6% priced the surprise is asymmetric: a hike is already in the price and a hold is not, so the larger move comes from the outcome nobody is positioned for — amplified by a dealer book still short gamma by $37.6B.

The Bank of Japan is the one that could hurt this book without any position being wrong. USDJPY is 153.57, -4.13% on the week and a fourth consecutive week of yen strength, with a hike 97% priced on a record ¥360tn of cross-border yen borrowing. Two central banks tightening in the same week, into negative gamma and a quarterly expiry, is the combination that turns an orderly repricing into a disorderly one.

Three things to check first on Monday. Whether PLTR's stop held on Friday; whether credit still refuses to worry — high yield has not moved in a week of 52-week highs in Treasuries, which is the most reassuring number anywhere in this brief; and whether heat is back under the cap, by a stop or by a decision.

world.title: The pipeline built in the 1980s to survive a closed Hormuz was shut by drones from Iraq.

items.html: Saudi Arabia suspended the East-West pipeline on 13 September after a drone strike Saudi authorities traced to Maysan province in south-eastern Iraq, near the Iranian border. The 1,200km line normally carries 4–5m barrels a day against a 7m maximum, running crude to Yanbu on the Red Sea. It exists precisely to bypass the Strait of Hormuz — and Hormuz flows are already down to roughly 6–9m bpd from over a fifth of global supply. Repairs are estimated at five to six weeks. Brent went above $105 and was quoted near $108. Both the chokepoint and its designed alternative are impaired at once.

Anthropic's Dario Amodei published an essay urging AI companies to deliberately slow the development of more capable models, and Sam Altman agreed. Semiconductors sold off — Nvidia, SK Hynix and Samsung futures all lower — and technology closed the worst sector at −1.49%. President Trump responded on Truth Social that the only guardrails needed are a 'STRONG AND SMART' president. The market's read was not that AI is over but that the capex cycle might slow, which is why Alphabet and Meta rose while the chipmakers fell — and why Palantir, which sells governance rather than compute, rose 3.64%.

The FOMC decides Wednesday 16 September with a hike above 90% priced. The Bank of Japan decides Friday 18 September with a hike from 1.00% to 1.25% 97% priced. Triple witching is the same Friday. Two central banks tightening inside three days, the second landing on the largest options expiry of the quarter, into a dealer book that is short gamma. A decision priced above 90% has an asymmetric surprise: the damage is in a hold, not a hike.

world.note: The through-line: the oil shock is feeding the inflation print that is feeding the rate decision. Petrol added 3.9% in August and took the headline with it. Wednesday is the Fed responding to a supply shock it cannot reach with a policy rate.

stance.title: The regime was right all week and it did not save a single position.

items.html: Policy Tightening, week 2. Friday's 3.4% CPI widened the binding gate's cushion rather than narrowing it, and Monday agreed: a 5% ten-year, a 52-week high in the two-year, a hike above 90% priced. Nothing argues against the regime. The regime simply had nothing to say about a fee-guidance cut or a seven-cent stop miss.

Net gamma −$37.62B — a 10 September figure, four sessions old, because the clone cannot be refreshed. Treat the level as indicative and the sign as the only tradeable part. Negative gamma into an FOMC decision tomorrow and a triple witching on Friday is the structural fact of this week.

Heat went 4.04R on Friday, 2.05R after the stops, and 3.05R once OKTA was on — back to a 3.0R cap, or 2.04R excluding the managed GOOG position. The round trip took one session. Nothing here is over the line, but the book is carrying full risk into a Fed decision tomorrow and a triple witching on Friday, with the newest position three days old. No room for another.

Two of the three positions in this book moved on Monday for the same reason. GOOG rose 3.06% as the AI-slowdown winner and OKTA 11.98% on the security bid — both are the Amodei essay, priced two different ways. AAPL, up 0.24%, is the only position not attached to it. That is not sector concentration, which a screener would catch; it is narrative concentration, which nothing in Phoenix measures. If Wednesday's Fed takes the tape back, or the safety story fades as quickly as it arrived, two thirds of the book moves down together.

Every one of these exits happened at the original stop. Nothing was widened, nothing was talked out of, nothing was averaged down. Two of them were losses and all three were correct executions — that distinction is the only part of this week that was under your control, and it went the right way.

stance.note: The honest read on the stance: it was right about rates and right about the direction of policy, and positions sized against that thesis still lost. Regime calls set the odds over a season. They do not immunise single names over three sessions.

macro.title: Five percent printed on the ten-year, and the pipeline built to avoid Hormuz is shut.

Monday's tape went well past all of it: the ten-year touched 5.00% intraday, the first time since October 2023, and closed 4.999%; the two-year set a 52-week high at 4.658%; the thirty-year held 5.354%. The front end moving with the long end is the market repricing the policy path, not term premium.

A hike on Wednesday is now priced above 90%, from 85-86% after Friday's CPI and roughly 70% before it. August CPI was +0.4% on the month and +3.4% on the year, both in line; core was +0.3%, a tenth above forecast, and +2.4% annually. Petrol did much of the headline work — up 3.9% to $4.28 a gallon on the Middle East — while shelter reaccelerated to +0.3% from +0.1%. The core detail is what moved the odds.

The pack's ten-year tracks daily. us02, real10 and hy still do not — all three read 0bp on the day for a sixth session — and hy is still quoted in percent rather than basis points. With the clone frozen, every one of these is Thursday's. Read the front end and credit at weekly resolution at best.

The dollar index closed near 99.5, up about 0.4%, on the yield move. USDJPY was ~154.3, off session highs near 154.9 — the yen gave back ground on Monday after four weeks of strength, which matters because the Bank of Japan decides Friday 18 September with a move from 1.00% to 1.25% 97% priced. Estimates put the yen carry trade at $764bn to $1.1tn. A BoJ hike landing on triple-witching Friday is the single most avoidable risk on this week's calendar.

High yield at 271bp once the unit switch is undone — inside the 300bp line that separates calm from watchful, and it has not moved through a week that produced a 5% ten-year. Credit is not pricing distress, which is worth holding onto: nothing that happened to this book was systemic. It is also Thursday's figure.

Phoenix has WTI at 102.48, +23.17% on the month. Monday's tape: WTI +2.25% to $102.30, Brent above $105 and quoted as high as $108, after Friday's brief dip under $100. Gold fell 1.76% to $4,331.40 — a geopolitical shock that pushed gold down, because real yields did the deciding. Bitcoin rose about 2.2% to ~$79,000.

macro.note: The gates. Three of four hold. items.html: This brief reported Gabriel's PLTR position as live on 11 September and again earlier this morning. It was not — it stopped out on Thursday 10 September. The reason is a method error, not a data gap: I was checking the closing price against the stop. PLTR closed Thursday at 165.86, comfortably above 164.62, and I wrote that the stop could not be confirmed. Its low that day was 164.55. A stop is an order that fills on the low, not a level tested at 4pm, and every position line in every brief before this one was checked the wrong way. From here the book is reconciled against intraday lows since entry, and the two remaining positions have been re-checked on that basis: GOOG's lowest bar since entry is 324.41 against a 305.67 stop, AAPL's is 309.90 against 301.99.

PLTR closes below its stop — the condition was written wrong. It never closed below its stop and it stopped out anyway. Written against a close, it was never capable of firing on the event it existed to catch. Replacing it: conditions on positions are now written against the low, and the diff should be too.

August CPI at or below 3.0% — FAILED, closed Friday. It printed 3.4% and the binding gate's cushion widened rather than narrowed. No dovish argument is left and Wednesday is above 90% priced. Retired.

A CEO speaking at a conference in the week before a quarter closes is a scheduled, knowable event. It belongs on the calendar.

If OKTA simply round-trips to where it traded on Friday, the position is −0.81R and the stop has not been touched. A 12% one-day move that is three days old can give all of that back in one session, and this one is not on the calendar — which is exactly what made BAC expensive.

The FOMC holds on Wednesday instead of hiking. Above 90% priced, so the surprise is one-sided. In a market short gamma by $37.6B — a stale figure, but the sign is not in doubt — a hold produces a rally larger than the news deserves and would be the first real challenge to POLICY_TIGHTENING since the regime was set on 31 August.

The Bank of Japan hikes on Friday into triple witching. 97% priced, 1.00% to 1.25%, on a carry position estimated at $764bn to $1.1tn, with USDJPY back at ~154.3 rather than the sub-150 this brief has been watching for. The risk is not the hike — it is the hike landing on the quarter's largest expiry while dealers are short gamma.

weekly.headline: The week the Fed stopped arguing with itself — and Palantir walked to its stop
weekly.standfirst: Four sessions, because Monday was Labor Day, and the index gave up about 0.6% across them — the third week running in which a great deal happened and the S&P barely moved. Underneath: crude through $100 on Saudi production at its lowest since 1990, the ten-year up 15bp to 4.94% with the thirty-year at levels last seen in June 2007, the VIX out of a 28-session range, and dealer gamma collapsing to −$44B before recovering. CPI then printed 3.4% in line on Friday and put a September hike at 85.6%, killing the dovish case this brief had been testing since 4 September. In the book AAPL turned green on a doubled revenue estimate and PLTR ended the week 0.75% above its stop after a Citigroup downgrade — whether it held is the open question of the weekend. Heat 4.04R against 3.0R.

Columns are the week to 2026-09-10 and entry-to-date; marks are Thursday's close because Friday is not yet in the engine.

The week's real event is a level, not a return. PLTR closed Thursday at 165.86, 0.75% above its stop, after Citigroup cut it to Market Perform on a P/E near 142 and BTIG went Neutral. Friday's close is not in Phoenix and I could not source one, so whether that stop held is the open question of the weekend. The Nasdaq rose 0.88% on the day, which makes a stop-out the less likely outcome — but 0.75% is inside this stock's ordinary intraday range, and if it has gone, heat falls to roughly 3.04R without a decision being made.

A Fed that stopped arguing with itself, and a stock that walked to its stop

1. The inflation question closed. CPI printed 3.4%% year over year against the 3.0%% test this brief had set as the first argument against POLICY_TIGHTENING — and it moved up from 3.3, not down. Odds of a hike at the 16 September meeting went from a coin flip a week earlier, to roughly 70%% on Thursday, to 85.6%% after the print. The regime's binding gate now clears its threshold by 0.9. There is no dovish case left to argue.

2. Dealer gamma collapsed and then partly recovered. Net gamma went −$3.98B on Tuesday, −$26.05B on Wednesday, −$44.19B on Thursday and −$37.62B in the latest pack. The index lost its 50-day on Thursday for the first time in this run. Friday's 1.06% rally on an in-line print is what that positioning does to ordinary news — and the same multiplier is pointed at Wednesday's decision. Phoenix's own diff never flagged any of it, because it tests for a sign flip and the sign was already negative.

3. Two positions resolved in opposite directions. AAPL launched the iPhone Duo at $1,999 — under the $2,000-plus that had been trailed — shipping 23 October, and the stock shrugged until Deepwater doubled its estimate of the Duo's share of fiscal 2027 iPhone revenue from 5%% to 10%%, sending it up 3.56%% and turning the position green. PLTR went the other way on a Citigroup downgrade, closing the week on its stop. Both were sell-side opinions rather than company news, which is worth noting: the book's two biggest moves this week came from analysts, not from the businesses.

4. Alphabet acquired a court. A US appeals court cleared 2,400–3,000-plus youth-addiction suits against Google, Meta, Snapchat and TikTok to proceed, and refused to delay the trial brought by 29 state attorneys general. That is materially larger than the FTC's YouTube probe this brief had been tracking, which remains unfiled after sixteen days. GOOG fell 2.09%% on the ruling and still finished the week as the book's steadiest name.

Oil stopped being a risk premium and became a supply number

WTI settled above $102 on Thursday and Brent reached $107.63, both through $100 for the first time since May, before Friday took WTI back to $99.05. The move was not a headline premium: Saudi Arabia reported production at its lowest level since 1990 after Houthi strikes on energy facilities including the 400,000 barrel-a-day Jazan refinery, and roughly ten commodity ships a day are crossing the Strait of Hormuz against a chokepoint that carries a fifth of world oil in peacetime. US petrol averaged $4.27 and diesel set a record.

The transmission into this book runs crude → CPI → the regime gate, and it worked all week. It also showed up somewhere more concrete: seven of the eight names in Phoenix's screener are now oil or marine shipping — DK, PBR, BP and PSX alongside BWLP, DAC and NMM. The war has stopped being a macro input and become what the screener returns. None of it is actionable while heat is over cap, and the screener has still reached nothing at its 20-bar horizon, so the verdict remains INSUFFICIENT.

Friday's 3.35%% fall in crude is the first thing to challenge that in two weeks. One down day from $102 is not a supply story ending.

Two central banks and an expiry, into a market that magnifies all three

FOMCFederal Reserve decision — a hike is 85.6% pricedWed2026-09-16
BOJBank of Japan decision — a hike is 97% pricedthis week2026-09-18
OPEXTriple witching — quarterly expiryFri2026-09-18

The Fed is the week. With a hike 85.6% priced the surprise is asymmetric: a hike is already in the price and a hold is not, so the larger move comes from the outcome nobody is positioned for — amplified by a dealer book still short gamma by $37.6B.

The Bank of Japan is the one that could hurt this book without any position being wrong. USDJPY is 153.57, -4.13% on the week and a fourth consecutive week of yen strength, with a hike 97% priced on a record ¥360tn of cross-border yen borrowing. Two central banks tightening in the same week, into negative gamma and a quarterly expiry, is the combination that turns an orderly repricing into a disorderly one.

Three things to check first on Monday. Whether PLTR's stop held on Friday; whether credit still refuses to worry — high yield has not moved in a week of 52-week highs in Treasuries, which is the most reassuring number anywhere in this brief; and whether heat is back under the cap, by a stop or by a decision.
